title: From Amritsar's Bylanes to Harvard's Stage: Vikas Khanna's Long American Vindication
excerpt: Harvard's South Asian Association has named the Michelin-starred chef its Person of the Year, the latest honor in a season that has turned Indian cuisine from curiosity into cultural force in America.
body:
Chef Vikas Khanna has spent a career insisting that Indian food belongs at the center of the American table, not its margins. This month, one of the country's most storied institutions agreed with him. The South Asian Association of Harvard University named the Amritsar-born, New York-based chef its **Person of the Year**, honoring a man who once cleaned apartments in Manhattan and now runs one of the city's most talked-about restaurants.

"What a milestone for Indian cuisine," Khanna said of the recognition. "To be named Person of the Year by Harvard University's SAA is beyond words. This recognition is not just an award — it's a promise. A commitment to continue honoring our culture through every dish, every detail."

## Context & Background

For the Indian diaspora, Khanna's biography reads almost like a parable. He was born in the crowded lanes of Amritsar, where his grandmother's kitchen and the city's Golden Temple langar — the free communal meal served to all comers — shaped his sense of food as something sacred and shared. He arrived in the United States with little, took whatever work he could find, and slowly climbed. He earned a Michelin star at Junoon in New York, authored more than forty books documenting India's regional cooking, directed the acclaimed film *The Last Color*, and during the pandemic mounted a relief effort that he says delivered more than 30 million meals across 135 Indian cities.

Earlier this year, *TIME* named him to its **2026 TIME100** list of the most influential people in the world. He has dedicated that honor, characteristically, to his grandmother, mother, and sister — "their sacrifices, blessings, and guidance" — rather than to himself.

## Current Developments

The Harvard recognition lands in a remarkable season for Indian food in America. In the most recent Michelin announcements, three Indian-origin chefs — Vijaya Kumar of Semma in New York, Chetan Shetty of Raina in Washington, and Sujan Sarkar of Indienne in Chicago — were awarded stars. Khanna, never one to compete quietly with his peers, celebrated all three publicly. "Diwali has arrived a little early in the United States," he wrote. "What an honor for India, our hospitality and cuisine."

At the heart of his own work is **Bungalow**, the Greenwich Village restaurant he opened to acclaim and a Michelin Bib Gourmand. Khanna has framed it less as a business than as a devotion. Asked why he refuses to franchise it across the globe, he answered that he builds each restaurant "with bhakti" — devotion — and that a diner should walk in and feel that "isme rooh hai," that it has a soul.

## Diaspora Impact

For Non-Resident Indians, Khanna's ascent carries a weight that goes well beyond restaurant reviews. A generation of immigrants grew up apologizing for the smell of their lunch, explaining the contents of a tiffin to puzzled classmates, watching "curry" flatten the vast grammar of regional Indian cooking into a single word. Khanna's stated ambition — "I want Indian cuisine to be seen as the local cuisine of America" — speaks directly to that experience of being asked, perpetually, to translate yourself.

"People of my generation often felt like the unwanted underdogs," he has said of the Harvard honor, "so to receive recognition on a global stage is a tremendous honour." He has repeatedly redirected the credit toward India's street vendors and home cooks — "the real patriots of our cuisine," in his phrase — the anonymous millions whose recipes he has spent a lifetime documenting and elevating.

## What's Next

Khanna's reach now extends well past the kitchen. He continues as a judge on Celebrity MasterChef India, a perch that has made him a household name across the subcontinent, and his new film *Imaginary Rain*, a culinary drama set in New York, is slated for release later this year. His nonprofit work, from pandemic relief to his foundation for South Asian children, remains central to how he describes his purpose.

For the diaspora, the trajectory is its own kind of statement. A boy from the bylanes of Amritsar now stands on the stage at Harvard, accepting an honor on behalf of every kitchen back home. The recognition is personal, but the message is collective: the food that immigrants once carried quietly in steel tins is, at last, being celebrated on its own terms.
